text.p: These are the leading stories in the Pakistani press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The incoming government of Nawaz Sharif is expected to reopen negotiations with the International Monetary Fund to convince it to revise upward the budget deficit target of four percent to five percent for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).
- Former prime minister Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party, routed in February 3 general elections, will take a final decision on February 15 whether to boycott the assemblies.
- Caretaker Prime Minister's adviser on finance Shahid Javed Burki said he hoped prime minister-elect Nawaz Sharif would continue the fiscal policies of the caretaker stability.
- The Economic Coordination Committee of the Cabinet approved a financial restructuring plan for the multi-million dollar Saindak Copper-Gold Project.
- A consortium of foreign private investors has been formed to bid for state-run Pakistan International Airlines whenever the Privatisation Commission announces its privatisation.
- The Karachi Stock Exchange has approved the prospectus of Saadi Cement and provisional trading will start on February 23.
- Pakistan will not achieve the 18 million tonnes wheat production target fixed for 1996/97 (July-June) due to high cost of inputs that is deterring farmers from sowing wheat.
- U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is considering a trip to India and Pakistan, which would be the first such substantive visit by a U.S. secretary of state in 14 years.
- Pakistan denied reports in a Hong Kong newspaper that a Lahore-based organisation was shipping religious material to incite unrest in northwestern China and Beijing had complained about it.
- Leading U.S. banks and brokerage houses, including Merill Lynch and Citibank, as well as Britain's Jardine Fleming, are interested in becoming members of the Lahore Stock Exchange.
